alternatives.root_cause: A downstream dependency of checkout (most likely cart or payment) slowed, and checkout's latency is just the wait propagating to the caller
alternatives.why_not: No downstream service alerted; a dependency slow enough to push checkout over a latency threshold would usually breach its own latency SLO and appear in the alerting set, and frontend also calls cart but did not alert.

alternatives.root_cause: A flagd-driven flag flip enabled a slow code path reached through checkout's dependencies
alternatives.why_not: checkout does not talk to flagd in this topology, and the flagd consumers that do (ad, cart, recommendation, product-reviews, fraud-detection) show no symptoms.

verdict.summary: checkout itself became resource-starved (CPU/thread-pool/connection saturation in its own process), so requests queued inside checkout and its latency rose while none of its dependencies degraded
verdict.reasoning: Only checkout alerts, and it alerts for latency rather than errors. The blast radius is just checkout's own fan-out plus its callers (frontend, frontend-proxy), which is what graph traversal produces from a single alerting node and does not by itself implicate any downstream. If one of checkout's dependencies (product-catalog, currency, cart, payment, shipping, email) had become slow, that dependency would normally trip its own latency alert and the caller set would be wider than just checkout's. Latency-only, confined to the service that owns the work, points at saturation inside checkout - exhausted worker threads/connection pool or memory pressure with GC thrash - where requests wait on internal queues rather than on a remote call.
